subtitle: A Spoon Full of 7x Value Makes the Medicine Go Down, and My Thoughts on Timing and Position Sizing
title: Snacking on Banking and Insurance
description: A Spoon Full of 7x Value Makes the Medicine Go Down, and My Thoughts on Timing and Position Sizing
body_html:
Disclaimer: By reading this article, you acknowledge and agree to the terms and conditions

Timing. Sizing. They have more to do with each other than you’d think.

What are the odds of “top-ticking” or “bottom-ticking” a name? Just look at the graph of cosine(x).

If you tried to “top-tick” cosine(x) on the way up at various points, good luck, nearly all of your attempts would end in tears. The same goes for trying to “catch a falling knife” on the downswing.

Individual stocks and the market as a whole follow a much more complicated regime than a simple cosine graph, but the one thing they share is that top-ticking and bottom-ticking is nearly impossible. My advice: don’t even try to do it.

Frankly, it isn’t just traders who try, companies do it as well with share repurchases. Take Designer Brands, for example. In Q3 of 2024 they spent $50.6 Million (a massive amount relative to the market cap) repurchasing shares at $6.59, leaving roughly $20 Million in capacity remaining on the existing authorization. The repurchase screamed “bottom tick” attempt. Shortly afterwards, the stock dropped to $5.00 a share in Q4, $4.00 in 2025 Q1, and into the low 2’s in 2025 Q2, before recovering to the present $3.60 - $3.80 range. DBI’s repurchase activity since 2024 Q3? Essentially zero.

People angrily shake their fists “If you spent $50 Million buying it back in the 7’s you should love buying it back at $3!” It’s a good point.

But ask yourself, how many times have you done the exact same thing? You buy a position, it dips to a level even more attractive than your original entry, you don’t add, and a few months later you wish you did. For me, way more often than I’d like to admit.

That’s why I think timing and sizing have a lot to do with each other. Once you understand that the odds you have timed the “bottom-tick” are slim, starting with a smaller position and leaving yourself with room to add at more attractive levels can come in handy. The worst thing that can happen is the name runs away from you, and you make slightly less than you would have if you bought your entire position at once.

If I’m looking to make something a 3% position, I’ll start at a third of the desired weight, 1%, and buy another third of the desired position (1%) over the next 5 days. I’m not a large trader and it isn’t a matter of liquidity, rather, it prevents me from rushing in at a top or blowing out at a bottom and making emotionally charged decisions. If you look back to Google at the low 160’s earlier this year and Google at 320 currently, bullish / bearish sentiment entirely dominated a few trading days. Spreading your buys / sells over a few days reduces the likelihood of making drastic decisions at emotionally charged moments (of course, you can always make exceptions for moments driven by earnings, regulatory issues, etc).

I like to use the last third of my “firepower” to add at more attractive levels if the price moves against my entry, or add to my position at higher levels upon a breakout. This might sound counterintuitive; why save capital to buy more of something once it is already moving higher? The purpose of retaining the last third is to avoid “dead money”. Doing this gives you the option to add at more attractive prices, or establish a full position by adding at higher levels once a breakout begins; chances are once the breakout begins it has room to run.

In a market that is increasingly momentum driven, this tactic helps ensure your capital is deployed when the risk to reward is most favorable, not just when you first got excited about a trade. If you have a focus on smaller cap US Equities, or Global Value names that tend to float around until the breakout finally begins, saving a third of your firepower to add at more attractive levels, or upon a breakout, ensures you don’t tie up capital in a value trap.

Now, three trades I’ve been adding to recently.

Trade 1:

Sector: Financials

Long Northeast Community Bancorp ($NECB)

Weight: 1.00%

Current Price: $20.37

Short Term Target: $21.50 - $22.50

Northeast Community Bancorp is a well-capitalized small bank specializing in construction lending in the greater New York City area. The stock sold off heavily after Mamdani’s election, but I think the fear is largely misplaced. Just 5% of NECB’s loan book is New York City Multifamily (a portion of which is rent-stabilized), demand for construction loans in Brooklyn and Orange / Sullivan county is through the roof, and the bank has boasted impeccable credit quality since 2009 with net-charge offs amounting to less than 0.05% of their loan portfolio.

Northeast Community Bancorp is a rarity these days, as it is one of the few banks geared to benefit from higher-for-longer interest rates. The vast majority of its construction loan book, $1.4 Billion (78% of total loans), is floating-rate, meaning that Net Interest Margin will compress as interest rates are continually lowered.

This will serve as a headwind in 2026 as construction loan yields decline, but Northeast Community Bank has an extremely high cost of deposits via CDs which will also decline and offset some of this move. NECB is sitting on its strongest capital position in years with a sizeable backlog of construction loans, so organic growth will also offset rate declines next year.

To be blunt, NECB is a pretty boring bank. They don’t have a magical source of low-cost deposits like Customer’s Bank does via CUBIX, but what I am really attracted to here is their history of outperformance and their low valuation.

Over the last 10 years, NECB has consistently outperformed the broader regional banking benchmark, boasting annualized returns of 15%. At $20.37, it currently sits at roughly 6.2x trailing earnings, and 7.3x forward earnings (assuming $2.80 in 2026). Most importantly, the stock trades at a hefty 18% discount to year-end Tangible Book Value of $25.30. Importantly, the stock is now trading at low levels where the company historically repurchased shares at in 2023 and 2024.

NECB is a tradeable name. It dipped to $15 in 2024 before roaring to $28 and providing a nice exit opportunity. I took a stab at it earlier this year at $22, and at $20.50 at just 7x forward earnings and significantly below year-end Tangible Book Value of $25 (also within the historical repurchase range), I think it is attractively valued to warrant a starter position.

I’ve sized it relatively small at 1.00% of my portfolio, and for good reason. With NECB you are getting exceptional value to compensate for low liquidity and outsized concentration risk. It also pairs well with pure rates down names such as Waterstone Financial and OP Bancorp. I think by adding a basket of undervalued names to your portfolio at smaller weights (<5% each), ideally less than 2% each, you can add value exposure while maintaining flexibility and eliminating outsized concentration risk.

I think NECB is attractively valued at $20.37, and even more so in the low 20’s and high 19’s so I am saving firepower to add more. I think the stock has upside to $21.50 - $22.50, which would still imply a very reasonable 7.7x-8.1x P/E and discount to Tangible Book Value, and that purchases below $21 represent an opportunity to add regional banking exposure to your portfolio at an extremely attractive multiple.

Trade 2:

Sector: Financials

Long American Integrity Insurance ($AII)

Weight: 1.00%

Current Price: $20.08

Short Term Target: $22.00 - $23.00

American Integrity is a rapidly growing Florida insurer with a specialization in new build homes. The stock recently swooned 20% after the founders sold 3 Million shares via a secondary offering, which priced at $20 just days after the stock was selling at $25. I think overall market conditions (equities were down 5% in a matter of days) and limited liquidity led to a poor reception, and that a much more fair value for American Integrity lies in the $22.00 to $23.00 range.

The company has strong underwriting capabilities, excellent customer service, natural growth tailwinds driven by the continual assumption of Citizens (State Run Insurer) policies, and growth opportunities in South Florida Area (which they currently have little exposure to). The company also stands to gain from recent Litigation Reform, and significantly lower 2026 Reinsurance pricing. At roughly 6.9x my 2026 EPS estimate of $2.90, American Integrity trades at a steep discount to the broader FL peer group (HCI Group, Universal Insurance Holdings, American Coastal, Slide), only Heritage trades at a lower multiple.

What I like about American Integrity is the growth potential, its minimal premium to year-end Book Value of $17 (as compared to many peers, who trade at 1.5x to 2.0x), and the strong insider alignment (even after the 3 Million share sale, insiders still own 7.5 Million shares, about 35% of the company).

I think the recent secondary offering creates an opportunity, its poor reception has anchored the stock at $20 and secondary “flippers” will likely cause steep resistance in the $20.50 - $21 range as they sell out for a small profit. Nonetheless, I think American Integrity will be a long term outperformer given the insider alignment, specialization in new build homes, and its significant room to grow and with AII, you are getting a below industry multiple in exchange for accepting lower liquidity and outsized geographical risk. Once again, as is the case for NECB, I think a small position in the $20.00 - $20.50 range allows you to gain sector exposure to insurance at an excellent multiple, provided you keep the position at a low overall weight to minimize the external risks (in this case, a hurricane).

Trade 3:

Options Put Selling

Short IREN December 2026 $10.00 Strike Puts ($1.12)

Weight: (Risk = 0.5% of Account NAV – Example: 1 Contract = $1,000 of Risk, on $250,000 account, trade size is 1 contract)

Short PRMB December 2026 $7.50 Strike Puts ($0.49)

Weight: (Risk = 0.5% of Account NAV – Example: 1 Contract = $750 of Risk, on $250,000 account, trade size is 2 contracts)

This trade involves a high amount of risk, and the returns are likely subpar if you have a cash account (since the treatment of shorts puts within a cash account consumes a lot of capital).

I’m not trying to begin an Option Sellers arc here. Nonetheless, I was surprised to see such high Implied Volatility on Primo Brands puts, and to a lesser extent, on IREN puts.

For Primo, I found the stock attractive at the $16.00 level, but switched to short puts for a more attractive risk to reward setup. While selling water isn’t the most attractive business, Primo brands currently trades at roughly 11x 2026 forecasted earnings of $1.40, and has a sizeable share repurchase authorization of roughly $200 Million. While a total implosion of the brand is possible, the company would need to significantly miss EPS and have debt issues – given the 2028 term loan is trading above par, it seems the bond guys are unconcerned. A share price below $7.01 (the breakeven on this trade is $7.50 minus 49 cents of premium) would represent a 56% decline below current levels, which I find highly unlikely.

Earlier this year, Primo was trading in the mid 30’s at a 22x multiple after Saratoga Water became a social media joke. The decline in the share price was warranted, but I think the options market is now concerned about a similar drawdown occurring in 2026, which seems less probable now that Primo is trading at a typical, even sub-industry, consumer staples multiple. If you have a cash account, selling a $7.50 put ties up $750 in cash, so the return on this trade would be roughly 6.5% over a year if the puts expire worthless, which honestly isn’t that attractive. I think this trade is better suited for experienced options traders with margin / portfolio margin accounts, who may want to sell a little tail-risk without tying up too much capital.

The way I like to size a trade like this is by asking myself, “how much of my account am I willing to lose if the underlying goes to zero”. For Primo, that’s 0.5%. As a result, my risk budget is 0.5% of NAV divided by the max loss on each contract of $701, and that’s how I size the trade. Many people have gotten slammed this year putting on similar trades on names such as Fiserv or Charter, I think Primo is a much more predictable business since, if there is one thing I am sure of in 5 years, everyone still drinks bottled water.

The IREN trade is a higher risk than the PRMB trade.

Right now, the main bottleneck within data centers isn’t lack of chips, rather, it’s lack of electrification. The larger cloud providers have simply run out of data center capacity, and are striking deals with smaller operators like IREN and CIFR (who previously mined bitcoin) to start hosting. IREN is a highly contentious stock on X, and I have no interest in wading into what I think it is worth. Some analysts say $125, others say $39.

It’s clear the options market is also pricing in significant uncertainty, given the December 2026 $10.00 Strike Puts trade for $1.16. One of the main unknowns about IREN and CIFR are “will they be able to tap the debt markets to finance the deals they struck?”

It’s certainly possible capital will dry up, but what I like about IREN is the fact that the data centers are worth more than book. The stock may jump around as sentiment shifts (personally, I think it is headed lower), but I don’t think it’ll be trading below its own Tangible Book Value of $10.17 a share. To express a view on this, I’ve sold some December 2026 $10 Strike Puts for $1.16 apiece. The maximum risk on this trade is $884 a contract ($10 minus $1.16 in premium), and selling these left-tails is almost like selling catastrophe insurance – I don’t think IREN goes below $10 unless it spectacularly blows up.

The company is sitting on a $1.8 Billion cash position, and may announce a fresh at-the-market program which might hurt the share price but ironically derisks the short options position: if IREN brings in fresh cash in the $30 - $40 a share range, the odds it implodes decrease. If IREN were to sharply collapse, I think there would be a data center investor interested in purchasing the data centers, staving off a total implosion. As with the Primo Brands trade, the most I am willing to lose if IREN goes to 0 is 0.5% of my account, as a result, I’ve sized the trade by dividing 0.5% of NAV by $884 risk per contract to determine the amount of puts I sell.

Conclusion:

NECB and AII come with significant geographical risk, PRMB is a falling knife, and IREN is a “battleground” stock with a lot of controversy over what it is worth. Not the upbeat conclusion you were hoping for, right?

The reason I say this is I think all of these trades provide an attractive risk to reward setup, and that by sizing a bunch of these favorable setups at a small weight, you can add “torque” to your portfolio without taking outsized concentration risk.

A good illustration of this, in my opinion, is the performance of smaller “regional” insurers relative to the broader S&P 500 Property and Casualty Benchmark. Mercury General (MCY – California), Kingstone (KINS – New York, mostly Long Island), Heritage Insurance (HRTG – FL, CA, NY), have beaten the index by hundreds (not kidding) of percentage points over the last 2 years.

I’ve discussed all of these names – the fundamentals were extremely compelling, but many larger investors were unwilling to get involved. Why? The outsized geographical concentration of each. My point is, as a smaller investor, you can diversify by making several individual bets at a smaller weight (<5% of your portfolio), and generate outsized returns relative to a broader benchmark by picking and choosing your spots and constructing a risk profile similar to the broader benchmark, with components at much more attractive valuations.

Within banking, CUBI has outsized exposure to the crypto industry via its large zero-cost deposit magnet, CUBIX, OPBK has significant exposure to California and “ethnic” deposit bases and is a clear rates down name, NECB is a rates up name with significant exposure to construction and New York, WSBF is a rates down name with a heavy reliance on mortgage originations, yet by combining all of them at smaller weights, you can get diversified regional banking exposure to Mortgage Origination, the Crypto Industry, and Rates Down via outperforming names at 7x-9x earnings, rather than by purchasing the broader benchmark which has almost the same risk profile, but at 12x earnings.

I’ve been adding to my AII, NECB, PRMB and IREN trades, and will provide regular updates as developments occur.

Lastly, wishing you all a happy and healthy Thanksgiving.
